name: Cross-Cultural Robustness of Framing & Anchoring Effects
aliases: Cross-Cultural Replication of Framing & Anchoring Effects
description: At least some classic judgment effects designers borrow from behavioral economics do not appear to be limited to Western student samples. The safest reading here is meta-scientific: framing clearly held directionally across many countries, while the anchoring side is genuinely more mixed -- present, but not a clean universal replication.
design_relevance_note: Relevant when teams ask whether a behavioral-bias playbook generalizes across locales: it argues against assuming either 'these effects are only Western' or 'they work identically everywhere' without checking the actual evidence.
myth_risk_note: Real cross-cultural replication evidence already exists in the corpus (Many Labs 2), which found the framing effect held across 36 countries at reduced magnitude -- rated low, not high, to avoid contradicting that established finding; some caution remains warranted since 'reduced magnitude across cultures' is itself a real qualification on the effect's universality. The anchoring side's 2026-09-09 addition (Adair et al. 2007) reinforces this same caution rather than changing it: a culturally-bounded applied manifestation, not evidence the mechanism doesn't exist.
prevalence_note: A meta-science integrity label rather than everyday UX vocabulary; mainly relevant to cross-market research, localization, and evidence-generalizability discussions, not routine interface reviews.

findings.description: A cross-cultural negotiation study found that early first offers had an anchoring effect that hindered joint gains for U.S. negotiators, but the same early-offer behavior instead functioned as information-gathering and generated HIGHER joint gains for Japanese negotiators -- the opposite pattern. This shows anchoring's real-world negotiation manifestation is culturally bounded rather than a universal mechanical response to a numeric anchor: the same behavior served a different psychological function (consolidation vs. information-gathering) across the two cultures. Complicates rather than confirms a simple universal-anchoring reading, without disputing that anchoring exists as a genuine cognitive phenomenon.
findings.source_title: The timing and function of offers in U.S. and Japanese negotiations.

findings.description: Across preregistered direct replications of 28 classic and contemporary psychology effects run in 125 samples spanning 36 countries (N = 15,305), replication effect sizes were systematically smaller than the originally published effect sizes (median Cohen's d fell from 0.60 in the originals to 0.15 in the replications), and only about half the effects reached conventional statistical significance in the same direction as the original. Despite this general replication shortfall, exploratory comparisons found little heterogeneity in effect sizes specifically between WEIRD and less-WEIRD cultural samples — cumulatively, variability in results was attributable far more to which effect was being studied than to the culture, sample, or setting it was studied in.
findings.effect_size: 54% of 28 replications significant, same direction as original (50% at strict p<.0001); median Cohen's d fell from 0.60 (original) to 0.15 (replication); little heterogeneity attributable to WEIRD vs. less-WEIRD sample split specifically
findings.source_title: Many Labs 2: Investigating Variation in Replicability Across Samples and Settings
findings.source_venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

findings.description: Many Labs 2's battery of 28 direct replications included Tversky & Kahneman's gain/loss framing effect (the 'Asian disease' paradigm already documented in this corpus as find-tversky-framing) as one of the tested effects, run across the study's 36-country, 125-sample design. Consistent with the study's aggregate pattern, the framing effect replicated in the same direction as the original demonstration but at a reduced magnitude relative to Tversky & Kahneman's original effect size; the study's exploratory WEIRD vs. less-WEIRD comparison found no meaningful sign that this reduction, or the effect's presence, was specific to the Western student samples the effect was first demonstrated in.
findings.source_title: Many Labs 2: Investigating Variation in Replicability Across Samples and Settings
findings.source_venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
